## The Museum of Almost

There was a museum in my city that most people never noticed, because its entrance was only visible when you were slightly lost.

It occupied a narrow storefront between a locksmith and a bakery that opened too late. I found it on a rainy evening, after taking a wrong turn behind the railway station. The door was painted the same green as the walls, and the brass sign above it was easy to mistake for a row of faded numbers.

**THE MUSEUM OF ALMOST**

Below that, in smaller letters:

**Open whenever you are ready to remember.**

I went in on a Tuesday in November, carrying an umbrella I had forgotten to open. A woman sat behind the reception desk, reading a paperback with a cracked spine.

“Admission is free,” she said, looking up. “Leave your regrets at the door, if you’d like. Most people carry them around too long.”

The first exhibit was a hallway.

Not a photograph of a hallway, either—an actual hallway, about six feet long, lit by a single yellow bulb. A handwritten sign hung at the entrance:

**A CORRIDOR YOU WALKED DOWN WHILE DECIDING WHETHER TO STAY.**

I stepped inside. The floorboards creaked in a convincing way. At the far end stood a door I did not recognize.

“That one isn’t open today,” the woman called.

“How do you know?”

She turned a page. “Because you haven’t decided yet.”

Beyond the hallway were rooms filled with glass cases. The contents were modest:

A pair of tickets to a concert that had been sold out.

A recipe altered by one spoonful of sugar.

The book you kept beside your bed but never finished.

A letter written, sealed, and hidden inside a drawer.

There was a case containing several loose fragments of conversation. I leaned close and heard fragments of my own voice saying things I had never said: *I don’t mind. I understand. Perhaps you’re right.*

Then a different voice replied, *No, I think we should.*

The conversation ended there.

I moved to the next case.

**THE JOB YOU APPLIED FOR BUT NEVER MENTIONED AGAIN.**

Inside lay a blank application form.

“Is that real?” I asked.

“It’s possible,” said the woman, who had come to stand beside me. “Most exhibits here are.”

“Possible things?”

“Almost things.” She looked toward the cases. “Not fantasies. Not things you merely wished for. The things that could truly have happened—one small decision earlier or later.”

I wandered deeper into the museum. There was a summer afternoon displayed beneath a warm glass light. Nothing happened in it. That was the exhibit: an afternoon without children, work, errands, or plans. An afternoon spent reading on the floor because the light was good.

There was a room where no one had ever argued. Two chairs faced each other, and the space between them glowed softly.

There was a suitcase packed but never carried downstairs.

There was a case labeled:

**A CONVERSATION THAT WOULD HAVE CHANGED EVERYTHING.**

It was empty.

I looked at it for a long time. “Where is it?”

“Some exhibits are still on loan,” the woman said.

Outside, the rain had stopped. Through the museum’s front window, I could see the bakery next door, still dark, and the black windows of the locksmith’s shop. The street looked ordinary, but I no longer trusted the word. Every shut door seemed to contain a different life. Every person passing beneath the streetlamps seemed to be walking away from some invisible choice.

At the end of the last room was an empty display case. Its label read:

**THE DAY YOU BEGIN AGAIN.**

The woman noticed me looking at it.

“That one stays empty,” she said.

“So I haven’t begun yet?”

“You have.” She handed me my umbrella. “You’re just still standing in front of the museum.”

Outside, the pavement shone. I had no idea which way home was, and for once I did not immediately consult a map. I turned left, past the bakery and a garden I had never noticed, toward streets I would have sworn belonged to another part of the city.

Nothing miraculous happened.

No doors opened. No brass signs appeared. No woman behind a desk told me that my life was about to change.

But for several blocks, I did not think of the detour as a mistake.
